ch02.s8i_01: The inside of the gate. Rıza's truck waits with its engine running. Exhaust mixes with the fog.
ch02.s8i_02: (from the cab window) Brother! The ones outside are calling you, the ones inside are waiting for you. And you're standing in the middle. You always were.
ch02.s8i_03: You think the middle's easy? The wind hits you from both sides.
ch02.s8i_04: Don't ask what's in the back. I didn't either. The delivery note says 'spare parts'. Spare parts aren't usually this heavy, though.
ch02.s8i_06: This is Demirtaş's job, brother. Cevdet only pointed at the door. I'm just turning the wheel.
ch02.s8i_07: Defne's voice carries from outside, through the loudspeaker, shaky but clear. It's the first time Kemal has heard his daughter's voice coming out of a crowd.
ch02.s8i_07_v1: Defne isn't outside. Kemal looks for her in the crowd, is glad not to find her, then ashamed of being glad.
ch03.it.ch03_s8_bollard.l1: A rusty mooring bollard. Someone has chalked on it: 'R + K, 1993'. The rain has washed half of it away; the other half stubbornly remains.
ch03.it.ch03_s8_bollard.l2: I wrote that. Kemal said 'it'll wash off'. It hasn't in thirty years. Some things don't wash off.
journal.ch03.ch03_s8_guard: The port guard was listening to football on his night radio. When I asked about forty-seven, he turned the volume up.
ch03.it.ch03_s8_guard.l1: The guard in his hut, a late match on the radio. 'Forty-seven? No idea.' He turns the volume up.
ch05.s8i_01: Kemal breaks the fire alarm glass with his elbow. No bell. The wires aren't there.
ch05.s8i_02: (on the phone) Emergency! Karaliman Parts Plant, cell three! Fire! There are people inside. I don't know how many. Hurry!
ch05.s8i_03: At the other end of the line a calm voice repeats the address. Kemal holds on to that calm for a moment; then he walks into the smoke.
ch07.s8i_k1: Dad, I still don't know which side of the gate you were on. But whichever side I was on, you were looking at it. That much I know.
ch07.s8i_k2: When your mother left she said, 'you only ever look at machines'. She was right. But I never looked at you the way I look at a machine. Never like I was hunting for a fault.
ch07.s8i_k3: I know. You looked at me like a sensor. When something came close, you stopped.
ch07.s8i_k4: Kemal laughs. For the first time in a year. He doesn't notice he's crying as he laughs; Defne notices, and doesn't say so.
ch07.s8i_d1: I took the envelope because Cevdet stood at my mother's door asking about her bracelets. That's not an excuse. Just… a reason.
ch07.s8i_d2: The barrels came all the way to the hospital, Uncle Rıza. The smell's still in my coat. A reason doesn't wash it out.
ch07.s8i_d3: It doesn't. But you hid that photo, and I saw the barrels. We both said something too late. Maybe together we'll be in time.
ch07.s8i_d4: Stand next to me at the gate tomorrow. Don't talk; just stand there. We'll talk about the rest later.
ch07.s8i_r1: Thirty years. When I climbed the cranes you'd catch me if I fell, remember? 'If I can't catch you, I'll jump too,' you used to say.
ch07.s8i_r2: But I never jumped, brother. Not when you opened the gate, not when you were looking for me. I always waited down below.
ch07.s8i_r3: If nobody waited down below, nobody would climb the crane, Rıza.
ch07.s8i_r4: Rıza tops up his tea. Kemal's too. Without asking, the way he has for thirty years.
ch02.s8j_01: Seven in the evening. A table has been dragged in front of the gate, a loudspeaker on top. Bayram, the union rep, taps the microphone twice.
ch02.s8j_02: Friends! Management is offering to sit down tomorrow. On one condition: the picket ends tonight, the gate opens in the morning.
ch02.s8j_02_v1: Friends! The gate opened today, you all know that. Now management says 'let's sit down, end the picket'. What have we got left?
ch02.s8j_03: We vote. Those who say sit down at the table, raise your hand. Those who say keep the picket going, don't. That simple.
ch02.s8j_04: (in Kemal's ear) Boss, whatever you do, half of them will do the same. You know that, right?
ch02.s8j_05: Half of the two hundred people are looking at Kemal. The other half at their own hands.
ch02.s8j_c1.up: Raise your hand: sit down at the table.
ch02.s8j_c1.down: Keep your hand down: the picket goes on.
ch02.s8j_c1.none: Put your hands in your pockets. Don't vote.
ch02.s8j_r1: Kemal's hand goes up. Twenty hands follow, then fifty. Bayram stops counting; there's nothing left to count.
ch02.s8j_r2: Kemal's hand stays at his side. A few raised hands start to drop, then hesitate. The vote splits down the middle; the picket goes on, split.
ch02.s8j_r3: Kemal puts his hands in his pockets. Everyone sees it. Nobody knows what it means; neither does Kemal.
ch02.s8j_06: Right. The decision's made, it's on record. Whatever happens tomorrow morning, tonight we're here together. The tea's on.
ch02.s8j_07: Boss, if you were a machine, I could never write your instruction manual. Come on, tea.
ch03.s8j_01: (from the crane, over the radio) Rıza! You again? Only two kinds of men are at the port at this hour: those who owe and those who lend.
ch03.s8j_03: I'm the third kind: the one up top. You can see everything from here. Who's carrying what where, who's handing envelopes to whom.
ch03.s8j_04: Forty-seven's been sitting there three days. Nobody's taken it. Even the customs man turns his head when he walks past. In other words, it stinks.
ch03.s8j_05: If it stinks, why doesn't anybody say something?
ch03.s8j_06: Somebody did. Last year a forklift driver said something. Now he works in a warehouse in Bursa. Sees his family once a week.
ch03.s8j_07: I didn't tell you anything, Rıza. The radio's broken anyway. You didn't hear anything but static.
ch03.s8j_08: The radio crackles and goes quiet. The crane starts turning again; a container in the air, a tiny truck beneath it.
ch04.s8j_01: Three plates on the table, a pot of pasta. On the TV, the evening news: 'Karaliman strike in its third day.'
ch04.s8j_02: Look, our gate! Look, that's the nose of my truck at the back. We're famous.
ch04.s8j_04: Why, brother? You always said 'nobody sees us'. Well, now they do.
ch04.s8j_06: I should write that down. Might come up in the Turkish paper.
ch04.s8j_07: Rıza laughs, Kemal doesn't, Defne tries to hide that she's laughing. The pasta goes cold. Nobody asks for seconds, but the pot empties.
ch04.s8j_08: Defne. Tomorrow morning… Have you decided what you're doing?
ch04.s8j_09: Not yet. I'll walk around a bit tonight, then I'll tell you. Promise.
ch05.s8j_01: Kemal? At this hour? This isn't your shift.
ch05.s8j_02: I've been put on nights, Hamdi. Nevin's orders. Somebody on the line before the opening.
ch05.s8j_03: Strange night. Two trucks have come in at the back ramp since this evening. I asked for paperwork; they said 'management knows'.
ch05.s8j_04: I've been a night guard for thirty-two years. When they say 'management knows', it means nobody does.
ch05.s8j_06: The back-ramp camera's been off for two days. 'Under maintenance.' You're the maintenance man, Kemal. Are you the one maintaining it?
ch05.s8j_07: Kemal doesn't answer. Hamdi pours a capful of tea from his thermos and holds it out. Kemal takes it and walks inside.
ch06.s8j_01: The waiting corridor. Plastic chairs, a 'No smoking' sign on the wall, three cigarette butts beneath it.
ch06.s8j_02: Nevin is sitting in the row opposite. She's pretending she hasn't been crying; she isn't managing.
ch06.s8j_03: They called me in too. I wrote the list, after all. And the barrels came in on my signature. My signature! I never even read that paper.
ch06.s8j_03_v1: They called me in too. They have photos of the file on my desk. Somebody took them. Whoever did… did the right thing. I never even read that paper.
ch06.s8j_04: Twenty years I read every single paper. Once I didn't. Just once.
ch06.s8j_05: A policeman opens the door and reads out a name. Not Nevin's.
ch07.s8j_01: Three weeks have passed. Three weeks in Karaliman: two funerals or none, one investigation, a great many drawn curtains.
ch07.s8j_01_v1: Three weeks have passed. Nobody died; in this town they call that a miracle. Miracles don't pay the bills, though.
ch07.s8j_02: The plant is closed. No wages have been paid. The corner shop has opened a new page in its credit book and written 'The plant' at the top.
ch07.s8j_03: Hasan at the corner shop said 'pay later'. Nobody will be able to pay later; he knows that. He writes it down anyway.
ch07.s8j_04: Every morning I wake at six. There's no shift to go to. I wake at six anyway; the body doesn't recognise the decision.
ch07.s8j_05: The truck's outside. Every morning I start it and listen for ten minutes. No load to haul. The engine runs anyway.
ch07.s8j_06: Tonight everyone would gather at the flat. Whoever was left.
ch01.s8k_01: In the corridor Hamdi, the night guard, is handing over his shift, thermos in hand. The same sentence at the same time for thirty years.
ch01.s8k_02: Quiet night, Kemal. Quiet, I say, but the arm in cell three lifted twice on its own. With nobody around.
ch01.s8k_03: On its own? Test mode should have been off.
ch01.s8k_04: Should have been. In this plant there's a corridor between 'should have been' and 'was'. I'm the guard of that corridor.
ch01.s8k_05: How's Defne? Exam coming up, I hear. My grandson's sitting it too. 'Grandad, did you ever take an exam?' he asks. 'Every night,' I tell him.
ch01.s8k_06: Defne's fine. Maths is eating her brain, but she's fine. Say hello to your grandson.
ch01.s8k_07: Hamdi swipes his card. The machine beeps once: out. Kemal swipes his: in. The plant lets one watch go and takes up another.
ch02.s8k_01: Six in the morning. As Defne leaves, the light is on in her father's room. Kemal is dressed, sitting on the edge of the bed, one shoe in his hand.
ch02.s8k_02: I'm going to the picket, Dad.
ch02.s8k_04: You're coming too. From the other side.
ch02.s8k_05: I carry the key, Defne. A key doesn't pick a side. It's on the side of whoever opens the gate.
ch02.s8k_07: Kemal puts on his shoe, ties the lace, says nothing. Defne pulls the door shut. Two sets of footsteps on the stairs, going the same way.
ch05.s8k_01: Dawn. The sky over Karaliman turns grey, then a pale pink. The gulls come down to the port as they do every morning.
ch05.s8k_02: The fire chief takes off his helmet and wipes his forehead. 'This fire didn't start by itself,' he says, looking at no one. 'I'm putting that in the report.'
ch05.s8k_02_v1: The morning shift gathers at the gate. Hamdi the guard is telling them what happened in the night; everyone listens, nobody wants to believe it.
ch05.s8k_03: Outside the gate, the people who got out of the fire sit wrapped in blankets. Someone from the neighbourhood brings simit, someone else tea. Nobody asks for money.
ch05.s8k_03_v1: Outside the gate, a jerrycan and police tape. Someone from the neighbourhood brings simit, someone else tea. Everyone is looking at the tape.
ch05.s8k_04: Hamdi pours the last tea from his thermos into whichever glass is empty. 'Thirty-two years,' he says. 'Never seen a night like it. Never wanted to.'
ch08.s8k_01: As the board members walk to their cars, they stop for a moment. The people at the gate haven't left. Nobody is chanting; they're just standing there.
ch08.s8k_02: Twenty years I walked in through this gate. First time I've looked at it from outside. It looks bigger from here.
ch08.s8k_03: Hamdi comes out of his hut, takes off his cap and wraps the chain round the gate with his own hands. He doesn't lock it. Just wraps it.
ch01.s8l_01: A banner is going up in the production hall: 'Karaliman's future: Smart Line 3.' Underneath, two men in suits are holding a tape measure.
ch01.s8l_02: One is arguing about where to tie the ribbon. The other about which door the deputy minister will come in through. Nobody looks inside cell three.
ch01.s8l_03: They've got a tape measure out for the ribbon. Nobody measured anything for the sensor.
ch01.s8l_04: The digital clock over the line: 23 hours 12 minutes to the opening. Someone has stuck a label next to it: 'The countdown has begun!'
ch02.s8l_01: The 'podium' is a door laid across two pallets. Defne looks at the steps. Three of them. The three longest steps in the world.
ch02.s8l_02: Don't be scared. Everyone's scared anyway. When a scared person speaks, every scared person listens.
ch02.s8l_03: I don't know what to say.
ch02.s8l_04: Say you don't know. Nobody here knows. If anyone did, we wouldn't be standing at a gate.
ch03.s8l_01: Containers in rows, in colours. Red, blue, yellow. At night they're all the same colour: shadow.
ch03.s8l_02: My dad used to say, 'if you want to know a load, smell it first, then weigh it, then read the paper last.' The paper's the last thing to lie.
ch03.s8l_03: There's a light in the dispatcher's window. From inside the office, a television and a drawer opening and closing.
ch04.s8l_01: Defne is coming home from prep school. No smell of lentils on the stairs; it's pasta. So her dad cooked.
ch04.s8l_02: Pasta means Dad's got something to say. Whenever he has something to say, he makes pasta. It cooks fast; there's no getting out of it.
ch04.s8l_03: Rıza's shoes outside the door. One without a lace. Always the same shoe, always the same missing lace.
ch08.s8l_01: The gate comes into view. The chain, the hut, the half-torn banner. The same for months; but this morning everything looks as if seen for the first time.
ch08.s8l_02: Hamdi wipes the window of his hut. 'Last shift,' he says. 'Mine too. Thirty-two years I've watched this gate; today it feels like the gate is watching me.'
ch01.s8m_01: The rule before going into the cell: lock, tag, test. Kemal hangs the padlock on the panel and clips on the yellow tag with his name on it.
ch01.s8m_02: Boss, you're putting a lock on but the arm's in test mode. There's still power to it. What's that lock locking?
ch01.s8m_03: The habit. If you don't fit the lock, one day not fitting it becomes the habit.
ch01.s8m_04: Put that in the manual too. 'Kemal says.' I'll be outside; if anything happens, I'll hit the emergency stop.
ch01.s8m_10: End of shift. The same tired boots in the locker room, going the other way this time. Everyone heading home, the smell of machine oil in their pockets.
ch01.s8m_11: Kemal opens his locker. Defne's photo is where it always is. He doesn't look at it today; he closes the door, then opens it again and looks.
ch01.s8m_12_v1: Boss, you wrote the report. Everyone's talking. What happens tomorrow?
ch01.s8m_12_v2: Boss, you signed. I saw. The arm's opening tomorrow, isn't it?
ch01.s8m_13: Tomorrow will be like today, Selim. We'll come in at six and fit the lock.
ch01.s8m_13_v1: I don't know, Selim. Tomorrow, don't stand next to that arm. Promise me: don't stand next to it.
ch02.s8m_01: Kemal looks over the crowd at the podium. From here his daughter is the size of a finger.
ch02.s8m_01_v1: Kemal looks over the crowd at the podium. Defne isn't there. The bus left long ago.
ch02.s8m_02: She talks with her mother's voice. Her mother used to talk like that: first she'd shake, then she'd stop, then everyone would go quiet.
ch03.s8m_01: Ferhat the dispatcher lowers his glasses to the tip of his nose. Three phones on his desk; two ringing, one he isn't looking at.
ch03.s8m_02: 'Rıza. Sit down. Don't sit. Whatever. Forty-seven goes tonight. You're taking it. And this envelope is yours.'
ch03.s8m_03: Ferhat, I've taken loads from you for twenty years. You never once gave me an envelope.
ch03.s8m_04: 'For twenty years nobody gave me an envelope either, Rıza. This month they did. So I'm giving you one. That's how the chain works.'
ch03.s8m_05: Who's at the end of the chain?
ch03.s8m_06: Ferhat doesn't answer. He picks up one of the ringing phones, says 'Yes, sir', and turns his back on Rıza.
ch04.s8m_01: Kemal stands at the stove. He lifts the lid of the pot, puts it back, lifts it again. There's nothing to check; he just wants his hands busy.
ch04.s8m_02: Brother, that lid's been up twenty times in three minutes. The pasta's too embarrassed to cook.
ch05.s8m_01: Kemal walks the length of the line. The conveyors are still, the robots asleep. But the ceiling vents are running; somebody left them on.
ch05.s8m_02: Vents on, fire doors wedged open, the alarm light dark. It takes a lot of care to leave a plant this carelessly.
ch05.s8m_03: There's a smell near cell three. Thinner. Familiar, and wrong.
ch06.s8m_01: The commissioner falls silent and closes the file. The strip light flickers once. The room is full of people who aren't there; one in the empty chair, the others in everyone's head.
ch07.s8m_01: The table is laid. The tea is brewed. The chairs pulled out. Nobody wants to be the first to sit; in the end they all sit down at once.
ch07.s8m_02: A plate of biscuits in the middle. Mother Hayriye sent them, with a note: 'Don't fight. And if you do, finish the biscuits.'
ch08.s8m_01: The board's cars line up in front of the gate. Tinted windows. Nobody gets out at first; first a piece of paper comes out, in a lawyer's hand.
ch08.s8m_02: There are six paragraphs on the paper. One says 'we thank our employees'. None of them contains a single name.
ch01.s8n_01: Nevin's office. The whole hall is visible through the glass. Three phones on the desk, a pair of ribbon scissors and an unopened file.
ch01.s8n_02: Sit down, Kemal. I'm going to tell you something, and then I'm going to say I never did.
ch01.s8n_03: If this line doesn't open, they sell the plant. The buyer's ready. A relative of Demirtaş. The buyer doesn't want the line, he wants the land. Land with a view of the port.
ch01.s8n_04: So whether the line opens or not…
ch01.s8n_05: If it opens we buy two years. In two years kids finish school, babies are born, debts get a bit smaller. Two years isn't nothing, Kemal.
ch01.s8n_06: Two years with a dead sensor.
ch01.s8n_07: We'll replace the sensor. After the opening. After the minister has gone. I promise.
ch01.s8n_08: Behind the glass the arm in cell three slowly traces an arc in test mode and stops. Nobody is under it. This time.
ch04.s8n_01: Kemal sinks into the armchair in the living room. He's trying to pull his boots off; his shoulder won't let him.
ch04.s8n_01_v1: Kemal sinks into the armchair. He's trying to pull his boots off; the shoulder the steel arm hit won't let him.
ch04.s8n_03: Defne crouches down and undoes the laces. She tries to remember the last time she took her father's boots off. Five years old, on a holiday morning.
ch04.s8n_04: How's Ece? Still talking about the call centre?
ch04.s8n_05: I don't know. Every day she says something different. Yesterday she said 'I'm going to run away'. I asked where to. She said 'to the exam'.
ch04.s8n_05_v1: She starts on Monday. Night shift. Like you. She asked me, 'How does your dad stand it?'
ch04.s8n_06: I don't stand it. I get used to it. There's a difference, but you can't see it from outside.
ch04.s8n_07: The second boot comes off. Kemal stretches his legs and closes his eyes. Defne sits on the floor for a while, looking at the hole in her father's sock.
ch05.s8n_01: Half past three. A car pulls up outside the plant. Nevin gets out in slippers, a coat thrown over her pyjamas.
ch05.s8n_02: Nobody told me. I found out from the news. I found out about my own plant from the news.
ch05.s8n_02_v1: The guard called. 'Nothing happened, but something was about to,' he said. What does that mean? Do you get up at three for something that didn't happen?
ch05.s8n_03: Nobody answers. Nevin tries to look in through the gate; a policeman takes her arm and gently pulls her back.
ch05.s8n_04: I'm the manager here. For twenty years. …Twenty years, manager of what?
ch06.s8n_01: My father was a worker too. At the shipyard. A welder. One day a steel plate fell; his leg was saved, his job wasn't.
ch06.s8n_02: When I joined the police I said, 'now I'll be the one asking for answers'. That was thirty years ago. Asking isn't hard. Getting an answer is.
ch06.s8n_03: Plenty of people have sat in this room. Everyone talked about someone else. Very few talked about themselves. I wonder which you'll be.
ch06.s8n_04: The commissioner stirs his tea. The spoon taps the glass three times. Then silence, heavier than the question.
ch07.s8n_01: An envelope is pushed under the door. Company letterhead. It begins 'Dear employee'; it doesn't say which one.
ch07.s8n_02: 'Our facility will open for the last time tomorrow at 07:00, and the board's decision will be announced to our employees at the gate. Your attendance is important.'
ch07.s8n_03: 'Your attendance is important.' The first time our attendance has ever mattered. On the last day.
ch07.s8n_04: Twenty years I attended every morning at six. I find out it mattered on the last day.
ch07.s8n_05: I'm not even one of their employees. They sent it to me anyway. So anyone with an address is an employee.
ch07.s8n_06: The letter stays in the middle of the table, next to the teapot. Nobody folds it; folding it would feel like agreeing.
ch08.s8n_01: (through a megaphone) Friends! The board has spoken. Now we speak. But one at a time. For twenty years nobody at this gate spoke one at a time; today let's.
ch08.s8n_02: First an old fitter spoke: forty years, three plants, one heart attack. Then a young woman: six months, one contract, zero security.
ch08.s8n_03: Then a child. He said his father's name and fell silent. For a while the megaphone hissed in his place.
ch08.s8n_04: Your turn. Everyone's looking at you.
ch01.s8o_01: (running in through the door) Boss! Boss, are you okay? I hit the emergency stop, or I didn't, I don't know, my hand was shaking!
ch01.s8o_02: You hit it. The arm didn't stop. The problem isn't your hand, Selim. The problem is the arm's ears.
ch01.s8o_03: I… I work next to that thing every day, boss.
ch01.s8o_10: Midnight. Karaliman is asleep; all but the plant chimney, the port cranes, and Kemal.
ch01.s8o_11: Tomorrow morning the minister arrives. The ribbon gets cut. The arm will either stop or it won't. And I'll either be there or I won't.
ch01.s8o_12: Kemal sets the alarm for six. Then half past five. Then he doesn't set it at all; he wasn't going to sleep anyway.
ch01.s8o_12_v1: Kemal tightens the last screw and looks at the calibration screen. Green. It's two in the morning. Too late to go home, too early to sleep.
ch02.s8o_01: At the edge of the picket an old woman sits on a stool, knitting. In front of her, a piece of cardboard: 'My husband 31 years. My son 9 years. Me 0 days.'
ch02.s8o_03: 'A scarf. If the strike ends, it's for my grandson. If it doesn't, we'll tie it to the banner. I add a row every day so it's long enough.'
ch02.s8o_04: The scarf is already over a metre long.
ch03.s8o_01: Seven in the morning. Rıza knocks on his mother's door. Before opening it, Mother Hayriye asks: 'Are you hungry?' Breakfast is ready before he can answer.
ch03.s8o_02: Your eyes are red. You haven't slept. Where's the truck?
ch03.s8o_03: At the door, Mum. Four wheels, plus the spare.
ch03.s8o_04: I didn't ask about the wheels. I asked about the truck.
ch03.s8o_05: Rıza takes an olive, puts the stone on the edge of the plate and doesn't answer. His mother doesn't ask again. The tea is brewed a second time.
ch05.s8o_01: The nine o'clock news: 'An investigation has been opened into last night's incident at a factory in Karaliman. Officials have made no statement.'
ch05.s8o_02: 'Officials have made no statement.' Karaliman knew that sentence by heart. This time, for the first time, it wasn't enough.
ch06.s8o_01: Night. Home. The evening news is showing the police station steps. The camera searches for a face, doesn't find one, and moves on to the weather.
ch06.s8o_01_v1: Night. Home. The evening news is showing the police station steps. A familiar face on the screen; a shaky voice, but clear.
ch06.s8o_02: The weather: fog tomorrow, clearing in the afternoon. In Karaliman, holding out until the afternoon is always the hard part.
ch07.s8o_01: The way home. The streetlights go out one by one again. But this time it doesn't feel like someone behind is switching them off; they're going out because morning has come.
ch08.s8o_01: Only the old knitting woman's stool is left in front of the gate. The scarf has been tied to the banner. Three metres. Like a flag in the wind.
ch04.s8p_01: When Defne comes back in, her father is leaning against the door frame with a cold glass of tea, waiting for her.
ch04.s8p_02: My father wanted me to study too. Finish high school, he'd say, then a trade. At fifteen I went to the port. I told him 'one year'.
ch04.s8p_03: How long did the one year last?
ch04.s8p_05: Whatever you choose, don't tell me 'one year'. There's no such thing as one year. You either go or you stay.
ch04.s8p_06: What would have happened if you'd gone?
ch04.s8p_07: I'd never have met your mother. You wouldn't exist. That's why I've never asked myself that question.
ch04.s8p_08: Kemal drinks the cold tea in one go and puts the glass in the sink. Defne washes it, dries it, puts it away. The last thing to do before a decision.
ch06.s8p_01: The commissioner lays three photos on the table. A close-up of the sensor. The crowd at the gate. The open door of container forty-seven.
ch06.s8p_02: Three photos, three people. Each of you is in one of them. None of you is in all three. That's how this plant burned.
ch06.s8p_03: In the corner of the sensor photo there's a fingerprint in the dust. In the container photo, the bumper of a truck. In the crowd photo, right at the front, a girl.
ch06.s8p_04: I said I wanted a name. What I really want is a story. The name comes at the end of the story. A name without a story is just an accusation.
ch07.s8p_01: Late afternoon, the doorbell rings three times. The downstairs neighbour brings a pot of stuffed peppers. The flat opposite, a tray of börek. Hasan from the corner shop, a bag of bread: 'I didn't put it in the book.'
ch07.s8p_02: In Karaliman, food arrives at houses in mourning. At houses on strike too. This house is both. There's no room left in the kitchen for another pot.
ch07.s8p_02_v1: In Karaliman, food arrives at houses on strike. There's no mourning in this house; but the neighbourhood brought food as if there were. There's no room left in the kitchen for another pot.
ch07.s8p_03: Who's going to eat all this?
ch07.s8p_04: Who's going to eat all this?
ch07.s8p_05: The dishes are laid out on the table. Nobody is hungry. But nobody leaves their plate empty; you don't turn away the neighbourhood's hand.
ch08.s8p_01: Candles are burning by the gate. Small, yellow, stubborn in the fog. Someone keeps relighting the ones that go out; nobody sees who.
ch08.s8p_01_v1: A few candles are burning by the gate; for the fourteen who were let go last year. Small, yellow, stubborn in the fog.
ch08.s8p_02: Familiar faces in the crowd: from the locker room, the picket fire, the harbour teahouse, the hospital corridor. Karaliman is a small town; everyone was there on someone's night.
ch08.s8p_03: A little girl is holding the corner of the banner. Her father says, 'let go, it's heavy.' She doesn't.
ch08.s8p_10: (taking the megaphone from Bayram) I don't work here. My dad did. I grew up in front of this gate. Today I stop growing up in front of it.
ch08.s8p_11: Next time we'll be inside. Or in front of another gate. But there'll be more of us. I promise.
ch08.s8p_12: Nobody claps. Everyone nods. In Karaliman applause is cheap; a nod is a promise.
ch01.s8q_01: The hall wakes up. The presses make their first strokes, the forklifts dance to their reversing beeps. The same music for twenty years.
ch01.s8q_02: I know this sound. Which machine is tired, which one's lying, I can tell by ear. Cell three is too quiet today.
ch01.s8q_03: Yellow-and-black tape around cell three. Someone has pinned a note to it: 'OPENING TOMORROW — DO NOT TOUCH.' Below, in pencil: 'Nobody does anyway.'
ch02.s8q_01: Night. The wood in the drum is running low. Someone breaks up a chair and throws it on the fire. Nobody objects; the chair belonged to the plant anyway.
ch02.s8q_02: Kemal stands on the far side of the fire. The strikers make room for him; they neither quite let him in nor quite leave him out.
ch02.s8q_02_v1: Kemal stands on the far side of the fire. Nobody makes room for him. The hand that opened the gate is not held out to the fire.
ch02.s8q_03: Come here, boss. The cold's the same cold for everyone. Whichever side of the gate you're on.
ch02.s8q_04: Kemal holds his hands out to the fire. Sparks climb into the dark and go out. Another night passes.
ch03.s8q_01: Rıza shuts the trailer door. Inside, the barrels stand side by side in silence; twenty of them, the same size, the same colour, the same silence.
ch03.s8q_01_v1: Rıza checks the trailer door. Locked. He didn't know what was inside; he had chosen not to. That's a load too.
ch03.s8q_02: Twenty barrels. Twenty families. No, don't think like that, Rıza. Twenty barrels are twenty barrels. That's all.
ch03.s8q_03: He starts the engine. A light blinks on the dashboard: 'Low fuel.' Rıza laughs. Everything's low: fuel, time, nerve.
ch05.s8q_01: In the locker room Kemal puts on his overalls. Defne's photo is in his locker. Tonight he looks at it for a long time; ninth grade, no exam nerves.
ch05.s8q_02: By tomorrow morning it'll all be over. The exam, the opening. One night. Just one more night.
ch06.s8q_01: A reporter's face in the glass of the door at the end of the corridor. A channel logo on the microphone; a young face, tired eyes.
ch06.s8q_02: Behind her a cameraman stubs out his cigarette and lifts the camera onto his shoulder. When the door opens, the light will come on. It always goes like that: first the light, then the question.
ch07.s8q_01: The tea is finished. The stuffed peppers are finished. It's past eleven. No paper on the table, no plan; just six o'clock tomorrow morning.
ch07.s8q_02: Nobody asks 'what are we going to do'. The question sits on the table, next to the closure letter.
ch08.s8q_01: Hamdi's thirty-two-year duty roster hangs in the window of the guard hut. The last line is empty. Someone fills it in, in pencil: 'Today. Everyone.'
ch01.s8r_01: In the corridor to cell three Kemal looks at the diagram on the wall. The arm's reach is outlined in red. Inside the red, a line of text: 'When no person is present.'
ch01.s8r_02: 'When no person is present.' All the safety rests on those words. And whether a person is present or not, the sensor decides.
ch01.s8r_03: A signature and a date in the corner of the diagram. Three years ago. Nobody has updated it since; the arm has been replaced twice.
ch02.s8r_01: The inside of the gate. Kemal sees his own face in the window of the guard hut: forty-one, the mark of the helmet, a key.
ch02.s8r_02: Everyone I know is outside. Everyone I know is inside. And I'm a key between the two.
ch03.s8r_01: Rıza pulls the truck up outside the dispatch office. The port lights tremble on the wet tarmac; each one a different coloured lie.
ch03.s8r_02: Kemal used to say, 'the port is honest at night, because it thinks nobody's watching.' Is nobody watching, I wonder?
ch04.s8r_01: Just after midnight Rıza puts his shoes on at the door. The laceless one is still laceless.
ch04.s8r_02: (whispering, to no one) Everyone in this house is waiting for something. One for the exam, one for the shift, one for me. And I'm waiting for morning.
ch04.s8r_03: The door closes quietly. A single set of footsteps on the stairs; one step lighter than the other.
ch05.s8r_01: Blue lights turn and turn in front of the gate. A police officer writes something in his notebook; reads it twice, then a third time.
ch05.s8r_02: At the door of his hut Hamdi explains that the cameras were off. The policeman asks 'who switched them off'. Hamdi doesn't answer; he doesn't know, but he can guess.
ch08.s8r_01: The fog lifts a little. Behind the gate the line comes into view: dismantled robots, empty conveyors, and a rectangular stain where cell three used to be.
ch08.s8r_02: Everyone looks at the stain. Nobody says anything. Then all eyes turn back to the gate, to the board, and to you.
ch06.s8s_01: A camera in the corner of the room, its red light on. Recording. Every word is written down somewhere; every silence too.
ch06.s8s_02: A glass of water on the table, a box of tissues. Three tissues missing. After questions, tissues are the most used thing in this room.
ch06.s8s_03: Drink some water. You can use the tissues too. Nobody looks. I won't either; the camera will, but it doesn't tell anyone.
ch07.s8s_01: The plant's chimney is visible from the window. No smoke for three weeks. Gulls have settled on top of it; for the first time it's theirs.
ch07.s8s_02: With no smoke from the chimney the town smells cleaner. But hungrier.
ch07.s8s_03: Nobody closes the window. The gulls' cries and the smell of the sea fill the room. Thirteen hours to six o'clock tomorrow morning.
ch03.s8t_01: At the foot of a container, a cat with her kittens. Port cats belong to nobody; they eat everyone's leftovers and tell nobody's secrets.
ch03.s8t_02: On the night shift too, are you? Off you go. I didn't see anything, and neither did you.
ch04.s8t_01: The kitchen clock's battery is nearly flat; the second hand hesitates at every tick, then carries on. Everyone in this house is a bit like that.
ch04.s8t_02: Dad, the clock needs a new battery.
ch08.s8t_01: The paper goes from hand to hand. Some read it, some fold it, some pocket it. An old fitter turns it over and starts writing a list on the back: names.
ch08.s8t_02: The list grows. The back of the paper fills up; someone tears a page from their own notebook. The board's six paragraphs end up underneath two hundred names.
ch05.s8u_01: The hall is dark. The green light of the exit signs falls on the floor; every arrow points the same way, towards the door.
ch05.s8u_02: Twenty years I've seen these arrows and never followed them. Tonight, maybe, for the first time.
ch05.s8u_03: The tea in his thermos is still hot. Hamdi's cap is in his pocket. Kemal takes a sip and walks to the head of the line.
ch07.s8u_01: Midnight. The dishes are done, the chairs pushed back in. The closure letter is still on the table; someone has set a tea glass on it, leaving a round stain on the paper.
ch07.s8u_02: The round stain has landed right on the words 'your attendance is important'. Nobody wipes it off.
ch02.s8v_01: At the back of the crowd a simit seller has set up his stall. 'Half price for strikers', his sign says. An hour later he's changed it: 'Free for strikers.'
ch02.s8v_02: An hour after that his stall is empty and he's holding one end of the banner himself.
ch08.s8v_01: The chairman of the board opens his car door, pauses, looks at the gate. For a moment he seems about to say something. Then he straightens his tie and gets in.
ch08.s8v_02: The cars disappear into the fog. Two hundred people and a sheet of paper are left at the gate; on the back of the paper, two hundred names.
